items.stem: In which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate?
items.answer: anaphase
items.markingKey: A. Spindle fibres shorten.

items.stem: A student claims: "Interphase is a resting phase." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Interphase is a metabolically active phase including growth, DNA replication and protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: Interphase is a metabolically active phase including growth, DNA replication and protein synthesis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Why is meiosis needed in sexual life cycles?
options: It halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores the diploid number.
items.answer: It halves the chromosome number so fertilisation restores the diploid number.
items.markingKey: D. Constant chromosome number.

items.stem:
Squashes were made of sections of a garlic root taken at different distances from the root tip. The number of cells in mitosis and the total number of cells in a field of view were counted.

Distance from tip / mm | Cells in mitosis | Total cells | Mitotic index
0.5 | 33 | 229 | 0.144
1.0 | 18 | 231 | 0.078
2.0 | 11 | 206 | ?
3.0 | 8 | 246 | 0.033
5.0 | 4 | 193 | 0.021

(a) Calculate the mitotic index at 2.0 mm. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mitotic index between 0.5 mm and 5.0 mm. [2]
An organism has a diploid number (2n) of 14. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can it produce by random orientation of homologous pairs?
Briefly describe onion root tip squashes in school laboratories and explain what it reveals about the mitotic index.
items.answer: Root tips are stained and squashed to observe chromosomes in different stages of mitosis. Counting cells in each phase shows the proportion of time spent in mitosis and the rate of cell division.
items.markingKey: Context (Root tips are stained and squashed to observe chromosomes in different stages of mitosis.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Counting cells in each phase shows the proportion of time spent in mitosis and the rate of cell division. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the mitotic index.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Sexual reproduction is more advantageous than asexual reproduction."
items.answer: Sexual reproduction is advantageous in changing environments, while asexual reproduction is better for rapid colonisation of stable ones.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: meiosis and fertilisation create variation, aiding adaptation to changing environments and resistance to parasites. Arguments against: asexual reproduction is faster, needs no mate, and preserves successful genotypes; meiosis breaks up favourable gene combinations; only half of individuals bear young. Supported judgement: Sexual reproduction is advantageous in changing environments, while asexual reproduction is better for rapid colonisation of stable ones.

items.stem: Explain how the mitotic index is determined and what it shows about cell division.
items.answer: Root tip, stain (toluidine blue/acetic orcein), squash; count cells in mitosis and total; MI = mitotic cells/total; high MI in meristems and tumours; time in phase = fraction × cycle length; sampling and identification errors.
items.markingKey: Root tip, stain (toluidine blue/acetic orcein), squash; count cells in mitosis and total; MI = mitotic cells/total; high MI in meristems and tumours; time in phase = fraction × cycle length; sampling and identification errors.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number"?
items.answer: non-disjunction
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of non-disjunction.

items.stem: Explain how meiosis generates genetic variation.
items.answer: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I creates new allele combinations; random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I gives 2ⁿ combinations; random orientation of chromatids in metaphase II; random fertilisation adds further variation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes in prophase I creates new allele combinations; random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I gives 2ⁿ combinations; random orientation of chromatids in metaphase II; random fertilisation adds further variation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between anaphase II and anaphase I.
items.answer: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate.
items.markingKey: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An onion root tip slide shows 24 cells in mitosis out of 300 cells. What is the mitotic index?
In a root-tip squash, 209 cells were counted: 21 in prophase, 12 in metaphase, 5 in anaphase, 2 in telophase and the rest in interphase. Calculate the mitotic index.
items.markingKey: Cells in mitosis = 40 (M1); MI = 40/209 = 0.191 (A1).

items.stem: In a root-tip squash, 265 cells were counted: 29 in prophase, 9 in metaphase, 8 in anaphase, 10 in telophase and the rest in interphase. Calculate the mitotic index.
items.markingKey: Cells in mitosis = 56 (M1); MI = 56/265 = 0.211 (A1).

items.stem:
Squashes were made of sections of a garlic root taken at different distances from the root tip. The number of cells in mitosis and the total number of cells in a field of view were counted.

Distance from tip / mm | Cells in mitosis | Total cells | Mitotic index
0.5 | 28 | 188 | 0.149
1.0 | 15 | 211 | 0.071
2.0 | 10 | 235 | ?
3.0 | 5 | 198 | 0.025
5.0 | 3 | 205 | 0.015

(a) Calculate the mitotic index at 2.0 mm. [1]
(b) Calculate the percentage change in mitotic index between 0.5 mm and 5.0 mm. [2]
(c) Describe the trend in mitotic index. [2]
(d) Explain the trend. [2]
items.answer: (a) 0.043 (b) -90.2 % (c) Mitotic index decreases with distance from the root tip. (d) The meristem just behind the tip contains actively dividing cells; further back cells elongate and differentiate and stop dividing.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 10/235 = 0.043 (A1). (b) [2] (0.015 − 0.149)/0.149 × 100 (M1) = -90.2 % (A1). (c) [2] Decrease with distance (A1); highest near tip (A1). (d) [2] Meristem near tip (A1); differentiation further back (A1).

items.stem: Which is a mutagen known to cause lung cancer?
items.answer: chemicals in tobacco smoke
items.markingKey: chemicals in tobacco smoke. Carcinogens.

items.stem: Why are cancer cells often targeted by drugs that disrupt the spindle?
options: The spindle is only in cancer cells.
Cancer cells divide frequently, so blocking mitosis affects them more.
items.answer: Cancer cells divide frequently, so blocking mitosis affects them more.
items.markingKey: C. Chemotherapy.

items.stem: Distinguish between oncogenes and proto-oncogenes.
items.answer: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that stimulate cell division when needed; oncogenes are mutated forms that are permanently active, stimulating uncontrolled division.
items.markingKey: Proto-oncogenes are normal genes that stimulate cell division when needed; oncogenes are mutated forms that are permanently active, stimulating uncontrolled division. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: An inherited mutation in BRCA1 increases breast cancer risk. Why?
options: BRCA1 is a tumour suppressor involved in DNA repair; one faulty copy makes loss of function more likely.
items.answer: BRCA1 is a tumour suppressor involved in DNA repair; one faulty copy makes loss of function more likely.
items.markingKey: D. Tumour suppressor.

items.stem: Rafael writes: "Cyclins are enzymes that phosphorylate proteins." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Cyclins are regulatory proteins that activate CDKs; the CDKs are the kinases.
items.markingKey: Cyclins are regulatory proteins that activate CDKs; the CDKs are the kinases. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline the phases of the cell cycle and explain how the duration of each phase can be estimated from observations of cells.
items.answer: G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation, mitosis, cytokinesis; count cells in each phase; fraction × total cycle length; assumptions (asynchronous population); sources of error.
items.markingKey: G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation, mitosis, cytokinesis; count cells in each phase; fraction × total cycle length; assumptions (asynchronous population); sources of error.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The spread of cancer cells from a primary tumour to other parts of the body, forming secondary tumours"?
items.answer: metastasis
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of metastasis.

items.stem: Why are several mutations usually needed before a cell becomes cancerous?
options: Cancer is caused by viruses only.
Multiple control mechanisms (oncogenes, tumour suppressors, apoptosis) must fail.
items.answer: Multiple control mechanisms (oncogenes, tumour suppressors, apoptosis) must fail.
items.markingKey: D. Multi-step process.

items.stem: Explain how cyclins control the cell cycle.
items.answer: Different cyclins accumulate at different stages; they bind and activate CDKs; active cyclin–CDK complexes phosphorylate target proteins, triggering events such as DNA replication or mitosis; cyclins are then degraded, so CDKs become inactive; this ensures events occur in the right order.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Different cyclins accumulate at different stages; they bind and activate CDKs; active cyclin–CDK complexes phosphorylate target proteins, triggering events such as DNA replication or mitosis; cyclins are then degraded, so CDKs become inactive; this ensures events occur in the right order. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: With reference to HeLa cells, explain how it illustrates loss of cell-cycle control.
items.answer: Cervical cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 continue to divide in culture today. Mutations and HPV proteins disable tumour suppressors, so the cells divide indefinitely.
items.markingKey: Context (Cervical cancer cells taken from Henrietta Lacks in 1951 continue to divide in culture today.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Mutations and HPV proteins disable tumour suppressors, so the cells divide indefinitely. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to loss of cell-cycle control.

items.stem:
The concentration of a mitotic cyclin (arbitrary units) was measured in a population of synchronised cells. Cells were observed entering mitosis when cyclin concentration was highest; shortly afterwards the cyclin concentration fell sharply.

Time / h | Cyclin concentration / AU
0 | 5
2 | 5
4 | 5
6 | 5
8 | 5
10 | 32
12 | 58
14 | 85
16 | 5

(a) State the time at which cyclin concentration was highest. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean rate of increase in cyclin concentration between 10 and 14 h. [2]
(c) Explain how this cyclin causes the cell to enter mitosis. [3]
items.answer: (a) 14 h (b) 13.2 AU h⁻¹ (c) Cyclin binds and activates a CDK; the cyclin–CDK complex phosphorylates proteins that cause chromosome condensation, nuclear envelope breakdown and spindle formation.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 14 h (A1). (b) [2] (85 − 32)/4 (M1) = 13.2 (A1). (c) [3] Binds CDK (A1); phosphorylation of targets (A1); mitotic events (A1).

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Cancer is mainly a disease caused by lifestyle."
items.answer: Lifestyle factors cause a large proportion of cancers, but genetics and chance also play major roles.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smoking, UV exposure, diet and alcohol increase mutation rates and cancer risk. Arguments against: inherited mutations (BRCA1) and random replication errors cause many cancers; ageing increases risk regardless of lifestyle. Supported judgement: Lifestyle factors cause a large proportion of cancers, but genetics and chance also play major roles. Markbands (7 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The overall pattern of chemical modifications (such as methylation and histone modification) on a cell’s DNA and histones"?
items.answer: epigenome
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of epigenome.

items.stem: Explain the difference between genetic changes and epigenetic changes.
items.answer: Genetic changes alter the base sequence of DNA (mutations); epigenetic changes alter gene expression through chemical marks such as methylation without changing the base sequence.
items.markingKey: Genetic changes alter the base sequence of DNA (mutations); epigenetic changes alter gene expression through chemical marks such as methylation without changing the base sequence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Why do monozygotic twins become more different with age?
options: Their epigenetic marks diverge due to different environments and random changes.
They have different genes from birth.
items.answer: Their epigenetic marks diverge due to different environments and random changes.
items.markingKey: B. Epigenetic drift.

items.stem: Using the Dutch Hunger Winter (1944–45) as an example, explain epigenetic effects of the environment.
items.answer: People exposed to famine before birth had different IGF2 methylation and higher rates of obesity and heart disease decades later. Nutrition during development altered methylation patterns, with lasting effects on gene expression.
items.markingKey: Context (People exposed to famine before birth had different IGF2 methylation and higher rates of obesity and heart disease decades later.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Nutrition during development altered methylation patterns, with lasting effects on gene expression. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to epigenetic effects of the environment.

items.stem: A drug inhibits histone deacetylase. What is the likely effect on gene expression?
options: Histones remain acetylated, so more genes are transcribed.
items.answer: Histones remain acetylated, so more genes are transcribed.
items.markingKey: B. Used in some cancer treatments.

items.stem: Explain how gene expression is regulated in eukaryotes, including epigenetic mechanisms.
items.answer: Transcription factors, promoters, enhancers; methylation of cytosine; histone acetylation/deacetylation; chromatin condensation; tissue-specific expression; environment (diet, temperature); inheritance of marks in mitosis; imprinting; twins; Dutch Hunger Winter.
items.markingKey: Transcription factors, promoters, enhancers; methylation of cytosine; histone acetylation/deacetylation; chromatin condensation; tissue-specific expression; environment (diet, temperature); inheritance of marks in mitosis; imprinting; twins; Dutch Hunger Winter.

items.stem: Which base is methylated in DNA methylation?
items.answer: cytosine
items.markingKey: A. Often at CpG sites.

items.stem: Why are methylation patterns maintained after DNA replication?
options: Methyl groups are part of the base sequence.
Enzymes copy methylation onto the new strand at hemimethylated sites.
items.answer: Enzymes copy methylation onto the new strand at hemimethylated sites.
items.markingKey: C. Maintenance methylation.

items.stem: "All cells in the body express all their genes all the time." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Each cell type expresses only a subset of its genes.
items.markingKey: Each cell type expresses only a subset of its genes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Identical twins develop different diseases in old age. Which explanation fits epigenetics?
options: Their methylation and histone modification patterns diverged with different environments.
items.answer: Their methylation and histone modification patterns diverged with different environments.
items.markingKey: D. Epigenetic drift.

items.stem:
The percentage methylation of the promoter of a tumour suppressor gene and the relative expression of the gene (mRNA, % of normal tissue) were measured in seven tumour samples.

Sample | Promoter methylation / % | Relative expression / %
1 | 6 | 97
2 | 29 | 69
3 | 39 | 64
4 | 66 | 32
5 | 70 | 34
6 | 72 | 31
7 | 80 | 25

(a) State the relative expression in the sample with the highest methylation. [1]
(b) Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between methylation and expression. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship shown. [2]
(d) Explain how promoter methylation reduces gene expression. [2]
items.answer: (a) 25 % (b) r = -0.99 (c) Strong negative correlation: as promoter methylation increases, gene expression decreases. (d) Methyl groups on cytosines block binding of transcription factors/RNA polymerase and recruit proteins that condense chromatin, so the gene is not transcribed.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 25 (A1). (b) [2] Use of calculator/formula (M1); r = -0.99 (A1). (c) [2] Negative (A1); strong (A1). (d) [2] Blocks binding (A1); condensed chromatin (A1).

items.stem: "Epigenetics shows that the environment is as important as genes in determining phenotype." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Epigenetics shows genes and environment interact closely; phenotype results from both, rather than one being more important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: methylation and histone changes respond to diet, stress and toxins; identical twins diverge in phenotype. Arguments against: the DNA sequence still sets the range of possible phenotypes; many epigenetic effects are small or reset each generation. Supported judgement: Epigenetics shows genes and environment interact closely; phenotype results from both, rather than one being more important. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: What is the water potential of pure water at atmospheric pressure?
items.answer: 0 kPa
items.markingKey: 0 kPa. The reference value.

items.stem: Why do red blood cells burst in pure water but plant cells do not?
options: Red blood cells lack a cell wall to resist expansion.
Red blood cells have no membrane.
items.answer: Red blood cells lack a cell wall to resist expansion.
items.markingKey: C. Cell wall.

items.stem: Explain the difference between solute potential and pressure potential.
items.answer: Solute potential is due to dissolved solutes and is always zero or negative; pressure potential is due to pressure on the water, positive in turgid cells and negative under tension in xylem.
items.markingKey: Solute potential is due to dissolved solutes and is always zero or negative; pressure potential is due to pressure on the water, positive in turgid cells and negative under tension in xylem. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A plant cell has a solute potential of -1500 kPa and a pressure potential of +400 kPa. Calculate its water potential and state the direction of net water movement when it is placed in a solution of water potential -300 kPa.
items.answer: ψ = -1100 kPa; water moves into the cell
items.markingKey: ψ = ψs + ψp = -1500 + 400 = -1100 kPa (A1); water moves from higher to lower ψ, so into the cell (A1).

items.stem: "Water moves from a more negative water potential to a less negative one." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential.
items.markingKey: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to determine the water potential of potato tissue and explain how the results are analysed.
items.answer: Cylinders, cork borer, equal size; sucrose series; blot and weigh; equilibration; reweigh; % change; graph; interpolation to zero; ψ = ψs of solution; controls: temperature, time, surface area; repeats.
items.markingKey: Cylinders, cork borer, equal size; sucrose series; blot and weigh; equilibration; reweigh; % change; graph; interpolation to zero; ψ = ψs of solution; controls: temperature, time, surface area; repeats.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The potential energy of water per unit volume relative to pure water at atmospheric pressure (ψ, in kPa or MPa); water moves from higher to lower ψ"?
items.answer: water potential
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of water potential.

items.stem: Explain why animal cells need to be kept in isotonic surroundings.
items.answer: Animal cells lack walls; in hypotonic solutions water enters and they swell and burst (haemolysis); in hypertonic solutions water leaves and they shrink (crenation); tissue fluid and plasma are kept isotonic by osmoregulation; medical solutions are isotonic.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Animal cells lack walls; in hypotonic solutions water enters and they swell and burst (haemolysis); in hypertonic solutions water leaves and they shrink (crenation); tissue fluid and plasma are kept isotonic by osmoregulation; medical solutions are isotonic. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: At incipient plasmolysis, what is the pressure potential of the cell?
items.answer: 0 kPa
items.markingKey: D. Protoplast just leaving the wall.

items.stem: Briefly describe wilting of lettuce leaves and explain what it reveals about turgor and water potential.
items.answer: Lettuce left out wilts but becomes crisp again when placed in water. Water loss lowers ψp and cells become flaccid; in water ψ outside is higher so water enters and cells become turgid again.
items.markingKey: Context (Lettuce left out wilts but becomes crisp again when placed in water.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Water loss lowers ψp and cells become flaccid; in water ψ outside is higher so water enters and cells become turgid again. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to turgor and water potential.

items.stem:
Potato cylinders were blotted, weighed and placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 24 hours at 25 °C, then blotted and reweighed.

Sucrose / mol dm⁻³ | Initial mass / g | Final mass / g | Change in mass / %
0.0 | 2.40 | 2.63 | +9.6
0.1 | 2.66 | 2.85 | ?
0.2 | 2.54 | 2.63 | +3.5
0.3 | 2.56 | 2.55 | -0.4
0.4 | 2.40 | 2.28 | -5.0
0.5 | 2.50 | 2.31 | -7.6
0.6 | 2.43 | 2.16 | -11.1

(a) Calculate the percentage change in mass at 0.1 mol dm⁻³. [2]
(b) Explain why percentage change in mass, rather than change in mass, was calculated. [1]
(c) Estimate the sucrose concentration that is isotonic with the potato cells. [2]
(d) Calculate the water potential of the potato cells using ψs = −CRT (R = 8.31 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, T = 298 K; result in kPa when C is in mol dm⁻³). [2]
items.answer: (a) +7.1 % (b) The cylinders had different initial masses, so percentage change allows fair comparison. (c) about 0.29 mol dm⁻³ (d) about -718 kPa
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (2.85 − 2.66)/2.66 × 100 (M1) = +7.1 % (A1). (b) [1] Different starting masses (A1). (c) [2] Concentration at 0 % change by interpolation (M1) ≈ 0.29 (A1). (d) [2] ψ = −0.29 × 8.31 × 298 (M1) = -718 kPa (A1); at isotonic point ψ tissue = ψ solution.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "non-disjunction"?
options: A protein that binds to specific DNA sequences such as promoters or enhancers and increases or decreases transcription of a gene
The expression of a gene depending on whether it was inherited from the mother or the father, controlled by methylation
The random orientation of pairs of homologous chromosomes at metaphase I, so that each gamete receives a random mix of maternal and paternal chromosomes
Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number
items.answer: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number
items.markingKey: D. "non-disjunction" is failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate during meiosis, producing gametes with an abnormal chromosome number.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "oncogene"?
options: A mutated gene that promotes uncontrolled cell division; derived from a normal proto-oncogene
Exchange of sections of chromatids between homologous chromosomes during prophase I of meiosis
Describes a plant cell that is full of water, with the cytoplasm pushing against the cell wall
The component of water potential due to pressure (ψp); positive in turgid plant cells, negative (tension) in xylem
items.answer: A mutated gene that promotes uncontrolled cell division; derived from a normal proto-oncogene
items.markingKey: A. "oncogene" is a mutated gene that promotes uncontrolled cell division; derived from a normal proto-oncogene.

items.stem: Which is an example of an environmental factor affecting gene expression?
items.answer: temperature affecting fur colour in Himalayan rabbits
items.markingKey: temperature affecting fur colour in Himalayan rabbits. Enzyme in fur pigment active only in cool areas.

items.stem: Why does a potato strip in pure water gain mass?
options: Pure water has a lower water potential.
Starch absorbs water by diffusion only.
Pure water has a higher water potential than the potato cells, so water enters by osmosis.
items.answer: Pure water has a higher water potential than the potato cells, so water enters by osmosis.
items.markingKey: D. Water moves down the gradient.

items.stem: Diego writes: "Interphase is a resting phase." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interphase is a metabolically active phase including growth, DNA replication and protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: Interphase is a metabolically active phase including growth, DNA replication and protein synthesis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between benign tumours and malignant tumours.
items.answer: Benign tumours remain localised and do not invade; malignant tumours invade tissues and spread by metastasis.
items.markingKey: Benign tumours remain localised and do not invade; malignant tumours invade tissues and spread by metastasis. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain how DNA methylation and histone modification regulate gene expression.
items.answer: Methylation of cytosine in CpG islands of promoters blocks binding of transcription factors and recruits proteins that condense chromatin, silencing genes; histone acetylation neutralises positive charges, loosening DNA–histone binding and allowing transcription; deacetylation and methylation of histones condense chromatin and repress genes.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Methylation of cytosine in CpG islands of promoters blocks binding of transcription factors and recruits proteins that condense chromatin, silencing genes; histone acetylation neutralises positive charges, loosening DNA–histone binding and allowing transcription; deacetylation and methylation of histones condense chromatin and repress genes. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Solutes move by osmosis." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Osmosis is the movement of water; solutes move by diffusion or transport.
items.markingKey: Osmosis is the movement of water; solutes move by diffusion or transport. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between anaphase I and anaphase II.
items.answer: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate.
items.markingKey: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A cell cycle lasts 20 hours. 45 % of cells in a sample are in G1. Estimate the length of G1.
items.answer: 9 hours

items.stem: A gene’s promoter is highly methylated in liver cells but not in pancreatic cells. Which is most likely?
options: The gene is absent from liver cells.
The gene is expressed in liver cells only.
The gene is expressed in both.
The gene is expressed in pancreatic cells but not liver cells.
items.answer: The gene is expressed in pancreatic cells but not liver cells.
items.markingKey: D. Methylation represses.

items.stem: Potato tissue gains no mass in 0.25 mol dm⁻³ sucrose. What does this show?
options: The tissue’s water potential equals that of the solution.
items.answer: The tissue’s water potential equals that of the solution.
items.markingKey: C. Isotonic.

items.stem: A species has a diploid number of 8. How many combinations of chromosomes are possible in gametes from independent assortment alone?
items.markingKey: C. 2ⁿ where n = 4 pairs.

items.stem: A sample of 500 asynchronously dividing cells contained 217 in G1, 126 in S, 61 in G2 and 96 in mitosis. The total cell cycle lasts 24 hours. Estimate the duration of each phase.
items.markingKey: Duration = (number in phase/total) × cycle time (M1): G1 217/500 × 24 = 10.4 h; S 6.0 h; G2 2.9 h (A1); M 4.6 h (A1).

items.stem:
The percentage methylation of the promoter of a tumour suppressor gene and the relative expression of the gene (mRNA, % of normal tissue) were measured in seven tumour samples.

Sample | Promoter methylation / % | Relative expression / %
1 | 7 | 102
2 | 18 | 90
3 | 25 | 69
4 | 38 | 59
5 | 59 | 42
6 | 65 | 30
7 | 85 | 6

(a) State the relative expression in the sample with the highest methylation. [1]
(b) Calculate the Pearson correlation coefficient between methylation and expression. [2]
(c) Describe the relationship shown. [2]
items.answer: (a) 6 % (b) r = -0.99 (c) Strong negative correlation: as promoter methylation increases, gene expression decreases.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 6 (A1). (b) [2] Use of calculator/formula (M1); r = -0.99 (A1). (c) [2] Negative (A1); strong (A1).

items.stem: A plant cell has ψs = −800 kPa and ψp = +300 kPa. It is placed in a solution with ψ = −700 kPa. Which way does water move?
options: Into the cell until ψp reaches zero
items.answer: Out of the cell
items.markingKey: B. Cell ψ = −500 kPa; water moves from −500 to −700 kPa.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Sexual reproduction is more advantageous than asexual reproduction."
items.answer: Sexual reproduction is advantageous in changing environments, while asexual reproduction is better for rapid colonisation of stable ones.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: meiosis and fertilisation create variation, aiding adaptation to changing environments and resistance to parasites. Arguments against: asexual reproduction is faster, needs no mate, and preserves successful genotypes; meiosis breaks up favourable gene combinations; only half of individuals bear young. Supported judgement: Sexual reproduction is advantageous in changing environments, while asexual reproduction is better for rapid colonisation of stable ones.

items.stem:
The concentration of a mitotic cyclin (arbitrary units) was measured in a population of synchronised cells. Cells were observed entering mitosis when cyclin concentration was highest; shortly afterwards the cyclin concentration fell sharply.

Time / h | Cyclin concentration / AU
0 | 5
2 | 5
4 | 5
6 | 5
8 | 32
10 | 58
12 | 85
14 | 5
16 | 5

(a) State the time at which cyclin concentration was highest. [1]
(b) Calculate the mean rate of increase in cyclin concentration between 8 and 12 h. [2]
(c) Explain how this cyclin causes the cell to enter mitosis. [3]
(d) Explain why the cyclin is rapidly degraded after mitosis begins. [2]
items.answer: (a) 12 h (b) 13.2 AU h⁻¹ (c) Cyclin binds and activates a CDK; the cyclin–CDK complex phosphorylates proteins that cause chromosome condensation, nuclear envelope breakdown and spindle formation. (d) To inactivate the CDK so the cell can complete mitosis and return to G1; ensures one division per cycle.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] 12 h (A1). (b) [2] (85 − 32)/4 (M1) = 13.2 (A1). (c) [3] Binds CDK (A1); phosphorylation of targets (A1); mitotic events (A1). (d) [2] CDK inactivation (A1); prevents repeated division/allows exit (A1).

items.stem: Describe how the environment can affect the phenotype of an organism through gene expression.
items.answer: Himalayan rabbit, hydrangea flower colour vs pH (not epigenetic), agouti mice, Dutch Hunger Winter, temperature-dependent sex determination in reptiles; mechanisms: methylation, histone modification, enzyme activity.
items.markingKey: Himalayan rabbit, hydrangea flower colour vs pH (not epigenetic), agouti mice, Dutch Hunger Winter, temperature-dependent sex determination in reptiles; mechanisms: methylation, histone modification, enzyme activity.

items.stem: "The water potential model fully explains water movement in plants." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: The model correctly predicts the direction of water movement but must be combined with membrane permeability and mass flow to explain rates.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: ψ = ψs + ψp predicts the direction of osmosis between cells and solutions; explains turgor, plasmolysis and xylem tension. Arguments against: water also moves by mass flow and through aquaporins whose regulation affects rates; ψ does not predict the rate of movement. Supported judgement: The model correctly predicts the direction of water movement but must be combined with membrane permeability and mass flow to explain rates. Markbands (8 marks): Markscheme points: award 1 mark for each valid, relevant point up to the maximum; points must be linked and explained, not listed. A clear, well-structured response with correct biological terminology and a conclusion that follows from the argument is required for full marks.

items.stem: Define the term "meiosis".
items.answer: A reduction division of a diploid nucleus into four haploid nuclei, each genetically different
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a reduction division of a diploid nucleus into four haploid nuclei, each genetically different. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: What do cyclins bind to and activate?
items.answer: cyclin-dependent kinases
items.markingKey: A. Cyclin–CDK complexes.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "gene expression".
items.answer: The process by which information in a gene is used to make a functional product such as a polypeptide
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the process by which information in a gene is used to make a functional product such as a polypeptide. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Why is the tension in xylem described as negative pressure potential?
options: Xylem is under high positive pressure.
Transpiration pulls water up, so the water is under tension below atmospheric pressure.
items.answer: Transpiration pulls water up, so the water is under tension below atmospheric pressure.
items.markingKey: D. Cohesion–tension.

items.stem: Distinguish between anaphase II and anaphase I.
items.answer: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate.
items.markingKey: In anaphase I homologous chromosomes separate to opposite poles; in anaphase II sister chromatids separate. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "All tumours are cancerous." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Benign tumours do not invade or spread and are not cancers.
items.markingKey: Benign tumours do not invade or spread and are not cancers. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between genetic changes and epigenetic changes.
items.answer: Genetic changes alter the base sequence of DNA (mutations); epigenetic changes alter gene expression through chemical marks such as methylation without changing the base sequence.
items.markingKey: Genetic changes alter the base sequence of DNA (mutations); epigenetic changes alter gene expression through chemical marks such as methylation without changing the base sequence. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between solute potential and pressure potential.
items.answer: Solute potential is due to dissolved solutes and is always zero or negative; pressure potential is due to pressure on the water, positive in turgid cells and negative under tension in xylem.
items.markingKey: Solute potential is due to dissolved solutes and is always zero or negative; pressure potential is due to pressure on the water, positive in turgid cells and negative under tension in xylem. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Interphase is a resting phase." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Interphase is a metabolically active phase including growth, DNA replication and protein synthesis.
items.markingKey: Interphase is a metabolically active phase including growth, DNA replication and protein synthesis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A sample of 800 asynchronously dividing cells contained 366 in G1, 266 in S, 122 in G2 and 46 in mitosis. The total cell cycle lasts 12 hours. Estimate the duration of each phase.
items.markingKey: Duration = (number in phase/total) × cycle time (M1): G1 366/800 × 12 = 5.5 h; S 4.0 h; G2 1.8 h (A1); M 0.7 h (A1).

items.stem: Briefly describe monozygotic twin studies and explain what it reveals about epigenetic drift.
items.answer: Older identical twins show greater differences in methylation patterns than young twins. Different environments and random changes alter epigenetic marks over a lifetime.
items.markingKey: Context (Older identical twins show greater differences in methylation patterns than young twins.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Different environments and random changes alter epigenetic marks over a lifetime. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to epigenetic drift.

items.stem:
Potato cylinders were blotted, weighed and placed in sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 24 hours at 25 °C, then blotted and reweighed.

Sucrose / mol dm⁻³ | Initial mass / g | Final mass / g | Change in mass / %
0.0 | 2.44 | 2.70 | +10.7
0.1 | 2.56 | 2.80 | ?

items.stem: An organism has a diploid number (2n) of 16. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can it produce by random orientation of homologous pairs?
A sample of 800 asynchronously dividing cells contained 363 in G1, 268 in S, 92 in G2 and 77 in mitosis. The total cell cycle lasts 24 hours. Estimate the duration of each phase.
items.markingKey: Duration = (number in phase/total) × cycle time (M1): G1 363/800 × 24 = 10.9 h; S 8.0 h; G2 2.8 h (A1); M 2.3 h (A1).

items.stem: A student claims: "All cells in the body express all their genes all the time." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Each cell type expresses only a subset of its genes.
items.markingKey: Each cell type expresses only a subset of its genes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Cancer is mainly a disease caused by lifestyle." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Lifestyle factors cause a large proportion of cancers, but genetics and chance also play major roles.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: smoking, UV exposure, diet and alcohol increase mutation rates and cancer risk. Arguments against: inherited mutations (BRCA1) and random replication errors cause many cancers; ageing increases risk regardless of lifestyle. Supported judgement: Lifestyle factors cause a large proportion of cancers, but genetics and chance also play major roles. items.stem: "Epigenetics shows that the environment is as important as genes in determining phenotype." To what extent is this view justified?
items.answer: Epigenetics shows genes and environment interact closely; phenotype results from both, rather than one being more important.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: methylation and histone changes respond to diet, stress and toxins; identical twins diverge in phenotype. Arguments against: the DNA sequence still sets the range of possible phenotypes; many epigenetic effects are small or reset each generation. Supported judgement: Epigenetics shows genes and environment interact closely; phenotype results from both, rather than one being more important.
